newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan links with Zaire rebels hard to disguise.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan links with Zaire rebels hard to disguise.

text.p: Tell-tale evidence contradicts insistent denials by the Rwandan army and rebels in eastern Zaire that they have no military links.
The shadowy but important role played by the Tutsi-dominated Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA) at critical moments during the six-week revolt is slowly emerging.

Despite a well-managed campaign to conceal the links, the RPA's participation was evident to aid workers and journalists when Zairean government forces lost the city of Goma, on Rwanda's border, earlier this month.
They saw units of the Rwandan army moving into Zaire during the fighting and saw them take on Zairean troops in Goma, alongside rebels who include many ethnic Tutsis.
One correspondent came across a Rwandan officer he knew having a celebration drink at a hotel in Goma -- clearly embarrassed to be discovered.
Rwanda has every interest in supporting the rebels and, in the view of some diplomats and aid officials, every right.

But the backing is politically ultra-sensitive. If officially confirmed it would mean Rwanda had waged an act of aggression against a neighbour and would promote the view that a "Tutsiland" is being carved out in Central Africa.
Zaire has no doubts and has formally accused the RPA of invasion. Only one of Zaire's allies, Gabon, has publicly denounced Rwanda's role.
A senior former African diplomat said the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), knowing how divisive the issue of Rwanda's support is, would not take sides.
"But this will be said in private. Of course everyone knows they are supporting the rebels," he told Reuters, declining to be quoted by name.

Oblivious to such high-powered politics, local drivers, interpreters and translators have had conversations with soldiers who admit they are Rwandans and frequently ask for messages to be passed to Kigali, the Rwandan capital.
One soldier, speaking to a journalist, pretended first to be a Zairean, then a Ugandan before finally admitting to being a Rwandan.
A resident of Gisenyi, inside Rwanda just across the border, said he joined the celebrations after Goma was "liberated".
"We boozed all night in Goma with the RPA celebrating that it was in our hands. In the morning, military police put us all on a truck and drove us back across the border," he added.
This week as hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees streamed into Gisenyi, a Reuters journalist and a Rwandan walked into what is officially Zairean rebel-controlled territory.

In civilian clothes and with a pistol at his hip, a "rebel" commander on the Zairean side of the border ordered the Rwandan back, on the grounds it was "Zairean territory" which he was forbidden to enter.
The Gisenyi resident later said he recognised the "rebel" commander and four out of five other armed men at the border as serving soldiers with the RPA who were based in Gisenyi.
"Only one was from Goma. But the rebels are our brothers. We look the same, speak the same languages, think the same and have the same problems. So what does it matter?" he said.
This view coincides with that of many of the foreign aid workers who believe Rwanda was entitled to help their rebel allies take control of Zaire's east.
"The international community never gave this country any space for a political solution," one aid official said.

The Zairean border provinces of North and South Kivu have been the platforms for armed incursions into Rwanda since 1994. Among the one million Rwandan Hutu refugees in camps in those provinces were tens of thousands of gunmen determined to fight their way back to power in Kigali.

They lost it in July 1994 after committing a genocide, killing up to one million minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus. The Tutsi-led rebels who won the civil war and are now in charge waited in vain for two years for the international community to disarm gunmen disguised as refugees.

"(The world) forced them to this: to face continued destabilisation of Rwanda or to regain military control of the exiled Hutu population and bring them back through a counter-insurgency operation," said the aid official, speaking on condition of anonymity on the grounds his agency's operations in Rwanda would be at risk if he was identified.
"That doesn't mean the whole thing was conducted entirely by the RPA but there was a significant RPA role," he added.
Rwanda's spokesmen refuse to admit the RPA role in the Goma operation.
They have only confirmed a small and brief raid into Zaire, further south from Cyangugu, to push back hostile forces.
They concede some of the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels in Zaire are former members of the RPA, fighting in the 1990-94 civil war inside Rwanda.
The rebels, who say their ultimate goal is to free the whole of Zaire from the rule of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, deny they are Rwanda's surrogates.
"We are made up from every ethnic grouping here (in Zaire) and we have not received help from Rwanda or any other country," rebel leader Laurent Kabila said this month.
